docs.text:

docs.title: Activation & Licensing
docs.text: Zume Editor is a paid app with a free trial. You buy a subscription on our website (all platforms), and activate the app with the license key we email you.

docs.title: Free trial
docs.text: The first launch starts a 30-day free trial with all features unlocked. No account or payment is needed. When the trial ends, buy a license to keep using the editor.

docs.title: Buying a license
docs.text: Purchase on the website for $49 / year (Windows, macOS and Linux all use the website). Payments are handled by Paddle, our reseller / Merchant of Record. After payment you receive a license key by email (format ZUME-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX).

docs.title: Activating
docs.text:
1. Open Zume Editor.
  2. Help → Activate License.
  3. Enter the email you purchased with and the license key.
  4. Click Activate.

The app verifies your license online, then keeps working offline; it re-checks quietly in the background from time to time.

docs.title: One license, up to 3 computers
docs.text: A single license works on up to 3 of your own computers (any mix of Windows, macOS and Linux), for one named user. Commercial use is allowed.

docs.title: Moving to another computer
docs.text:
If you reach the 3-device limit or replace a machine:

  1. On the old computer: Help → Deactivate This Device.
  2. On the new computer: Help → Activate License with the same email and key.

docs.title: Managing or cancelling your subscription
docs.text: Help → Manage Subscription opens your secure Paddle portal page, where you can update payment details or cancel. Cancelling stops future renewals; you keep access until the end of the period you already paid for.

docs.title: Refunds
docs.text: We offer a 14-day money-back guarantee. If you are not satisfied, email support@smolt-stage.com within 14 days of purchase for a full refund. See Support.

docs.title: When a subscription ends
docs.text:
When a subscription is cancelled or a renewal fails, the app keeps working for a short grace period, then prompts you to activate again. Your files are never locked or altered - only the editor's licensed features stop until you renew.

docs.title: Macros
docs.text:
Record a sequence of edits and movements and replay it.

  • Record (Ctrl+Shift+U), Play (Ctrl+U), and play N times.
  • Save named macros, play them from a list, and bind them to F-keys.
  • Macros are saved in a documented text format you can edit.

docs.title: Lua scripting
docs.text:
Run Lua scripts against the current document (Script → Run Lua File, or Run Last Script). Scripts run in a sandbox (no file, OS or network access) and every edit a script makes is a single undoable step.

Scripts work in text, large-file and hex tabs. Sample scripts ship with the app: sort_lines, remove_duplicate_lines, trim_trailing_whitespace, count_words, list_todos, number_lines, uppercase_selection, fullwidth_to_ascii, csv_to_markdown_table and more.

docs.title: The zume API
docs.text:
Scripts talk to the document through a global zume table. Byte offsets are 0-based; a range is [begin, end).

Function Description zume.text() The whole document as a string zume.size() Document size in bytes zume.caret() The caret's byte offset zume.set_caret(pos) Move the caret zume.selection() Two values: begin, end of the selection zume.select(begin, end) Set the selection zume.selected_text() The selected text zume.insert(pos, text) Insert text at an offset zume.replace(begin, end, text) Replace a byte range zume.line_count() Number of lines zume.line(i) Line i (0-based), without its line ending zume.read(offset, len) A bounded read (for large-file tabs) zume.log(msg) Write a line to the script log zume.api_version The API version (2)

docs.title: Example scripts
docs.text:
Uppercase the selection (or the whole document when nothing is selected):

local b, e = zume.selection()
if e <= b then b, e = 0, zume.size() end
local text = zume.text():sub(b + 1, e)
zume.replace(b, e, text:upper())
zume.log(("uppercased %d bytes"):format(e - b))

Sort the selected lines (whole document when nothing is selected), as one undo step:

local size = zume.size()
local b, e = zume.selection()
if e <= b then b, e = 0, size end
local text = zume.text()
while b > 0 and text:sub(b, b) ~= "\n" do b = b - 1 end   -- widen to line starts
while e < size and text:sub(e, e) ~= "\n" do e = e + 1 end
local block = text:sub(b + 1, e)
local trailing = block:sub(-1) == "\n"
if trailing then block = block:sub(1, -2) end
local lines = {}
for line in (block .. "\n"):gmatch("(.-)\r?\n") do lines[#lines + 1] = line end
table.sort(lines)
local out = table.concat(lines, "\n")
if trailing then out = out .. "\n" end
zume.replace(b, e, out)
zume.log(("sorted %d lines"):format(#lines))

Remove duplicate lines, keeping the first occurrence and the original order:

local text = zume.text()
local seen, out, removed = {}, {}, 0
local trailing = text:sub(-1) == "\n"
if trailing then text = text:sub(1, -2) end
for line in (text .. "\n"):gmatch("(.-)\r?\n") do
  if seen[line] then removed = removed + 1
  else seen[line] = true; out[#out + 1] = line end
end
local result = table.concat(out, "\n")
if trailing then result = result .. "\n" end
zume.replace(0, zume.size(), result)
zume.log(("removed %d duplicate line(s)"):format(removed))

Number every line (" 12: text"), using line_count / line:

local out, count = {}, zume.line_count()
for i = 0, count - 1 do
  out[#out + 1] = ("%4d: %s"):format(i + 1, zume.line(i))
end
zume.replace(0, zume.size(), table.concat(out, "\n"))
zume.log(("numbered %d lines"):format(count))

Tip

An AI assistant can write these scripts for you. See MCP → Let the AI write a Lua script.

docs.title: Project hooks
docs.text: A project can run a script on open and before save (on_open / on_save in the project settings), and keep project-local macros and scripts.

docs.title: CLI (zume-cli)
docs.text:
A command-line companion, zume-cli, ships alongside the app (next to the executable on Windows, in bin/ on Linux, and in the app folder on macOS). It reuses the editor's own engines, so results match the GUI.

Microsoft Store (MSIX) build

The Microsoft Store build does not make zume-cli usable from the command line. Its files are installed under the protected C:\Program Files\WindowsApps\… folder (a version-specific path that changes with every update and is not on your PATH), so zume-cli cannot be run or scripted directly. To use the CLI — or the MCP server — on Windows, install the portable ZIP (or the installer build) instead, extract it to a stable folder, and run zume-cli.exe from there.

zume-cli <command> [arguments] [flags]

The commands below are the complete set. zume-cli is a deliberately small headless subset of the editor (the full tool is the app itself); there is no --version, and running it with no arguments or an unknown command prints the usage and exits with code 2.

docs.title: Global flags
docs.text: Flag Effect Applies to --regex Treat the pattern as a regular expression (default: literal) find, search, replace --ignore-case Case-insensitive match (default: case-sensitive) find, search, replace

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Success 1 Runtime error (prints error: <message> to stderr - e.g. file not found, bad regex) 2 Usage error (wrong arguments; prints usage)

docs.title: find - search one file
docs.text:
zume-cli find <pattern> <file> [--regex] [--ignore-case]
Prints one line per match as file:line:column (1-based), then a summary N match(es).

docs.title: search - recursive find in files
docs.text:
zume-cli search <pattern> <dir> [glob] [--regex] [--ignore-case]
Searches dir recursively. glob optionally restricts file names (e.g. *.cpp). .git, build and node_modules are always skipped. Prints file:line:column: preview per match, then N match(es) in M file(s) (with (truncated) if the result cap was hit).

docs.title: replace - replace-all in one file
docs.text:
zume-cli replace <pattern> <replacement> <file> [--regex] [--ignore-case]
Replaces every match and saves the file in place (regex back-references like $1 work in --regex mode). Prints N replacement(s). The file is written only when at least one replacement was made.

docs.title: aikey - gen-AI API keys (for the MCP hub)
docs.text:
Manage the named API keys that the MCP http_request tool injects. Keys are kept in the OS credential store, never in a file.

zume-cli aikey set <name> [value]     # store a key (prints: stored '<name>')
zume-cli aikey list                   # list key names, one per line
zume-cli aikey remove <name>          # delete a key (prints: removed '<name>')
If you omit value for set, the key is read from standard input so it is not left in your shell history.

docs.title: cloud - cloud drives
docs.text:
Work with files on Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive and Box. The refresh token is kept in the OS credential store (never a file), and is shared with the editor - a login here or in the app works in both.

zume-cli cloud <provider> login ...          # authorize and save the token
zume-cli cloud <provider> ls [path]          # list a folder (root by default)
zume-cli cloud <provider> get <remote> <local>   # download a file
zume-cli cloud <provider> put <local> <remote>   # upload a file
zume-cli cloud <provider> logout             # forget the saved token

<provider> is dropbox, googledrive, onedrive or box. The login arguments differ by provider (you supply your own OAuth app's credentials):

zume-cli cloud dropbox     login <app_key>
zume-cli cloud googledrive login <client_id> <client_secret>
zume-cli cloud onedrive    login <client_id>
zume-cli cloud box         login <client_id> <client_secret>

Dropbox shows a code to paste back; Google / OneDrive / Box open a browser and capture the redirect on a local port (register http://localhost:53682/callback as the redirect URI in your OAuth app). zume-cli dropbox ... still works as an alias for zume-cli cloud dropbox ....

docs.title: geo - map / geospatial data
docs.text: Reuses the editor's geo engine (see MAP). File conversions read a file and print the result to stdout; coordinates may be given as decimal degrees or DMS (e.g. 35°41'N).

docs.title: Format conversion
docs.text:
zume-cli geo geojson2wkt <file>
zume-cli geo wkt2geojson <file>
zume-cli geo geojson2kml <file>
zume-cli geo kml2geojson <file>
zume-cli geo geojson2gpx <file>
zume-cli geo gpx2geojson <file>
zume-cli geo geojson2csv <file>
zume-cli geo csv2geojson <file> [lonCol latCol]
csv2geojson auto-detects the longitude/latitude header columns; if it cannot, pass the two 0-based column indices (lonCol latCol).

docs.title: Measurement
docs.text:
zume-cli geo length <file>     # geodesic length in metres  (GeoJSON or WKT input)
zume-cli geo area   <file>     # geodesic area in square metres

docs.title: Coordinate operations
docs.text: Command Arguments Output geohash <lat> <lon> [precision=9] the geohash string unhash <geohash> lat, lon jpr <lat> <lon> <zone> northing, easting (Japan Plane Rectangular CS, zone 1-19) unjpr <X> <Y> <zone> lat, lon tile <lat> <lon> <zoom> z/x/y quadkey=… bbox=west,south,east,north dms <lat> <lon> decimal lat, lon reproject --from <epsg> --to <epsg> <file.geojson> reprojected GeoJSON (via PROJ)

docs.title: convert - file conversion
docs.text:
zume-cli convert                      # list every converter id
zume-cli convert <id> <in> [out]      # convert a file (stdout if out is omitted)

<id> is a converter such as base64.encode, csv.toJson, json.toYaml, gzip.compress, bzip2.compress, html.toMarkdown. Markdown / HTML to PDF has its own ids and always needs an output file:

zume-cli convert md.toPdf   notes.md   notes.pdf
zume-cli convert html.toPdf page.html  page.pdf

See File conversion & archives for the full list and the in-editor equivalents.

docs.title: archive - zip / tar / 7z archives
docs.text:
zume-cli archive list    <archive>                 # list entries
zume-cli archive extract <archive> [dest-dir]      # extract (default: current dir)
zume-cli archive create  <archive> <path>...       # create from files / folders

create picks the format from the extension: .zip, .tar, .tar.gz / .tgz, .tar.bz2 / .tbz2, .tar.xz / .txz, .7z. extract also reads .rar and .xz (read-only). Encrypted archives are not supported.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
zume-cli find TODO src/main.cpp
zume-cli search "fn\s+\w+" src --regex --ignore-case
zume-cli replace http:// https:// config.ini
zume-cli aikey set openai            # then paste the key at the prompt
zume-cli geo csv2geojson points.csv
zume-cli geo geohash 35.68 139.76 8
zume-cli geo reproject --from 4326 --to 3857 area.geojson
zume-cli convert json.toYaml config.json config.yaml
zume-cli convert md.toPdf README.md README.pdf
zume-cli archive create site.tar.gz public/
zume-cli archive extract bundle.7z out/

docs.title: CloudDrive
docs.text:
Open and edit files stored in your cloud storage accounts:

  • Dropbox
  • Google Drive
  • OneDrive
  • Box

Connect an account with Remote → CloudDrive and sign in through the provider's own secure sign-in (OAuth) - Zume Editor never sees your cloud password. Browse the drive in the sidebar, open a file in a tab, and save to upload it back.

Note

CloudDrive is for consumer cloud storage. For your own servers, use Remote Files (SFTP / FTP / FTPS).

docs.title: You provide your own OAuth app credentials
docs.text: Zume Editor does not ship a built-in cloud client. The first time you connect a provider you enter your own OAuth app's credentials (a Client ID, and for most providers a Client Secret). You create that app once, in the provider's developer console - it is free, takes a few minutes, and the credentials are stored in your OS credential store (never in a file), shared with zume-cli.

docs.title: The redirect URI
docs.text:
Google Drive, OneDrive and Box finish the sign-in by redirecting to a small local server Zume Editor runs. Register this exact redirect URI in your app:

http://localhost:53682/callback

A mismatch here is the most common setup error (redirect_uri_mismatch). Dropbox uses a paste-the-code flow instead and needs no redirect URI.

docs.title: Connecting the first time
docs.text:
1. Remote → CloudDrive → Connect to <provider>.
  2. Enter the Client ID, then the Client Secret (Dropbox asks only for the app key; OneDrive only for the Client ID).
  3. Your browser opens the provider's consent page - approve access. (Dropbox shows a code to paste back into the editor instead.)
  4. Zume Editor catches the redirect on localhost:53682 (within ~3 minutes) and saves the token. The drive appears in the sidebar.

Next time, the saved token is reused - no browser step - until you Remote → CloudDrive → Disconnect (or logout in the CLI).

docs.title: Where to get the Client ID / Client Secret
Google Drive
docs.text:
1. Open the Google Cloud Console and create or select a project.
  2. APIs & Services → Library → enable Google Drive API.
  3. APIs & Services → OAuth consent screen → set it up (User type External; while the app is in Testing, add your Google account under Test users).
  4. APIs & Services → Credentials → Create credentials → OAuth client ID → Application type Web application.
  5. Under Authorized redirect URIs add http://localhost:53682/callback.
  6. Create it, then copy the Client ID and Client secret.

docs.title: Dropbox
docs.text:
1. Open the Dropbox App Console → Create app → Scoped access, and choose Full Dropbox or App folder.
  2. On the app's Permissions tab enable the file scopes (read and write).
  3. Copy the App key from the Settings tab. (Dropbox uses the paste-the-code flow, so no redirect URI and no secret are needed.)

docs.title: OneDrive
docs.text:
1. Open the Azure Portal → App registrations → New registration.
  2. Add a redirect URI http://localhost:53682/callback (as a Mobile & desktop / public client - no secret is used).
  3. Grant the delegated Files.ReadWrite permission.
  4. Copy the Application (client) ID.

docs.title: Box
docs.text:
1. Open the Box Developer Console → Create New App → Custom App → User Authentication (OAuth 2.0).
  2. Set the redirect URI to http://localhost:53682/callback.
  3. Copy the Client ID and Client Secret from the app's Configuration.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
zume-cli cloud googledrive login <client_id> <client_secret>
zume-cli cloud dropbox     login <app_key>
zume-cli cloud onedrive    login <client_id>
zume-cli cloud box         login <client_id> <client_secret>

zume-cli cloud <provider> ls [path]
zume-cli cloud <provider> get <remote> <local>
zume-cli cloud <provider> put <local> <remote>
zume-cli cloud <provider> logout

The CLI uses the same loopback sign-in and shares the saved token with the editor. See the Command Line page for details.

docs.title: Compare files
docs.text: Compare → Compare With File opens a two-pane diff. Both panes are editable and re-diff live, so you can resolve differences by editing or by taking a block from the other side (merge). Navigate differences with F7 / Shift+F7.

docs.title: Compare folders
docs.text: Compare → Compare Folders walks two trees and lists each path as same, different, left only or right only. Open a file from the list to diff it.

docs.title: Byte compare
docs.text: For binary files, Compare Bytes With File aligns both files as hex rows.

docs.title: Merge conflicts
docs.text: Open a file with Git conflict markers and use Merge → Next/Previous Conflict and Take Ours / Theirs / Both to resolve each conflict as one undo step.

docs.title: File conversion & archives
docs.text: Zume Editor converts text and data between many formats, exports Markdown / HTML to PDF, and creates and extracts zip / tar / 7z archives — from the editor and from the zume-cli command line.

docs.title: Convert a file
docs.text:
Convert: Convert File… (in the command palette / Tools) lists every converter. Pick one and choose where to save; the result is written to the file you pick. The active document is the input.

Available converters:

Group Converters Text encodings Base64 / Base64URL encode·decode, URL encode·decode, HTML-entity encode·decode, Unicode escape·unescape, ROT13, Base32 encode·decode Tokens JWT decode Data CSV ↔ JSON, CSV ↔ TSV, CSV → Markdown table, CSV → HTML, CSV → SQL, JSON ↔ YAML, JSON ↔ TOML, JSON ↔ INI, JSON minify / pretty, HTML → Markdown Compression (single stream) gzip, zlib and bzip2 — compress / decompress

Note

gzip / zlib / bzip2 here compress one file into one stream. For multi-file .tar.gz / .tar.bz2 archives, see Archives below.

Tip

To chain several of these over the selection in place (for example base64.decode | gzip.decompress | json.pretty), use Code → Apply Convert Recipe… — see Transform recipes, which lists every step the recipe accepts.

docs.title: Export to PDF
docs.text:
A Markdown or HTML document can be saved as PDF:

  • File → Export to PDF…, or the to PDF entry in the Convert File picker, or the CLI (below).
  • A save dialog asks where to write the .pdf.
  • Rendering uses the platform's own engine (Windows: the Edge WebView2 runtime; macOS: Core Graphics; Linux: Pango / Cairo), so Japanese and other scripts render with the system fonts.

docs.title: Archives
docs.text:
Create and extract archives from the folder panel (right-click a file or folder):

  • Extract Here — on an archive file, extracts into a sibling folder named after the archive.
  • Compress… — on a file / folder (or a multi-selection), asks where to save; the extension you choose picks the format.
Format Extract Create .zip ✅ ✅ .tar, .tar.gz / .tgz, .tar.bz2 / .tbz2, .tar.xz / .txz ✅ ✅ .7z ✅ ✅ .rar / RAR5 ✅ — .xz ✅ —

Note

RAR is extract-only (the format is proprietary). Encrypted RAR / 7z is not supported. A .7z entry whose name is non-ASCII may not round-trip through the 7z container (the file contents are unaffected).

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
# Conversion
zume-cli convert                      # list all converters
zume-cli convert <id> <in> [out]      # convert a file (stdout if no out)
zume-cli convert md.toPdf   in.md  out.pdf
zume-cli convert html.toPdf in.html out.pdf

# Archives
zume-cli archive list    <archive>
zume-cli archive extract <archive> [dest-dir]     # default: .
zume-cli archive create  <archive> <path>...      # format by extension

create writes .zip, .tar, .tar.gz / .tgz, .tar.bz2 / .tbz2, .tar.xz / .txz and .7z; extract also reads .rar and .xz. See the Command Line page for the full CLI reference.

docs.title: CSV & Data Grid
docs.text:
Open a .csv or .tsv file to edit it as a grid - rows and columns instead of raw text - while the file on disk stays plain CSV.

  • Edit cells directly; add and remove rows and columns.
  • The delimiter is detected; quoting and escaping follow RFC 4180.
  • Switch between the grid and the raw text view at any time.

docs.title: Customization
docs.text:
Open Tools → Settings for the main options, or edit the settings file directly.

  • Themes - Light, Dark, High Contrast, or your own theme file. The app can follow your OS high-contrast setting.
  • Toolbar - choose which commands appear, and reorder them.
  • Menus - add commands to the built-in menus.
  • Keybindings - rebind commands to your own shortcuts.
  • Language - English or Japanese (more to come).
  • Font & zoom - Ctrl++ / Ctrl+- / Ctrl+0, or Ctrl+wheel.
  • Layout - split panes, dockable panels, a split file panel, word-wrap by file type, and more.

docs.title: Database
docs.text: Connect to a database, browse its schema and run queries from inside the editor, with results shown in a grid.

docs.title: Supported databases
docs.text:
SQL

Engine Notes Default port SQLite Local database file, or a new / in-memory database — (file) MySQL / MariaDB Also MySQL-compatible servers (e.g. TiDB) 3306 PostgreSQL Also PostgreSQL-compatible servers 5432 Microsoft SQL Server Over the native TDS protocol 1433

NoSQL

Engine Notes Default port Redis RESP protocol 6379 MongoDB MongoDB wire protocol 27017

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
• SQLite - open a database file (e.g. .db / .sqlite), or create a new one.
  • Server engines - provide host, port (leave it at the default to use the engine's standard port), user, password and, optionally, a default database. TLS is used by default for networked engines.

Credentials are protected

Connection passwords are stored in your operating system's secure credential store (Windows Credential Manager, macOS Keychain, Linux Secret Service), never in plain settings or session files. See Privacy & Security.

docs.title: Working with a connection
docs.text:
• Schema browser - tables and views with their columns, types, primary keys and indexes; and, for engines that have them, functions, stored procedures, triggers and sequences.
  • Run SQL - write a statement and run it; results appear in a grid (large result sets are capped and marked truncated). For statements that change data, the number of affected rows and the execution time are reported.
  • Inline edit - edit result cells; writes use parameterized statements, so values (text, numbers, blobs, NULL) are bound safely without hand-quoting.
  • NoSQL - Redis and MongoDB connections run commands / queries and show the results in the same panel.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Is there a free trial? Yes - 30 days, all features, no account needed. See Activation.

How much does it cost? $49 per year, purchased on our website (all platforms).

How many computers can I use one license on? Up to 3 of your own computers, in any mix of Windows, macOS and Linux.

Can I move my license to a new computer? Yes - Help → Deactivate This Device on the old one, then activate on the new one.

Does it work offline? Yes. It verifies online when you activate and re-checks occasionally, but works offline in between.

Which operating systems are supported? Windows 10/11, macOS and Linux.

How do I cancel, and can I get a refund? Cancel from Help → Manage Subscription. We offer a 14-day money-back guarantee - see Activation and Support.

Where are my settings and logs stored? Locally on your machine - see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: A quick tour so you can find your way around.

docs.title: The window
docs.text:
• Tabs - each open file is a tab. Drag to reorder; Ctrl+T opens a new tab, Ctrl+W closes one.
  • File panel (sidebar) - toggle with Ctrl+B. Browse folders, Recent and Projects; it has an Explorer-style tree with detail columns.
  • Editor area - split a tab into two panes (vertical/horizontal), or show two different files side by side.
  • Bottom / side panels - search results, the Terminal, compare output and more. Panels are dockable.
  • Status bar - line/column, language, encoding, line ending and more. Click the encoding or language to change it.

docs.title: First steps
docs.text:
1. Open a file or folder - Ctrl+O, or drag files onto the window.
  2. Edit - type as usual. Undo/redo is Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y.
  3. Find - Ctrl+F for the find bar; Ctrl+R for the full Find & Replace dialog. See Search & Replace.
  4. Save - Ctrl+S.

docs.title: The command palette
docs.text: Press Ctrl+Shift+P to open the command palette — the fastest way to find and run anything in the editor. Start typing part of a command's name and the list filters by a fuzzy match (so "fif" finds Find in Files); ↑ / ↓ move the selection, Enter runs it, Esc closes. Each row shows the command's keyboard shortcut, if it has one, so the palette doubles as a way to learn shortcuts. Recently run commands rise to the top, and you can pin favourites (favorite_commands in settings — see Customization). Commands that do not apply to the current tab are shown greyed. Almost every feature in this guide has a command, so when you cannot find a menu item, search the palette for it.

docs.title: Panels: docking, moving and floating
docs.text:
The bottom and right dock areas hold panels — search results, the Terminal, FTP / SFTP / SSH browsers, compare output and more. Each panel is a tab in its area, and you can rearrange them to suit your screen:

  • Move a panel between the bottom and the right area by dragging its tab, or right-click the tab and choose Move to Right / Move to Bottom (the View menu has the same commands).
  • Float a panel out into its own window — to put a Terminal on a second monitor, say — with Panel: Float Tab (right-click the tab, or the View menu / palette). The floating window keeps updating live as its content changes.
  • Re-dock a floating panel by closing its window (its title-bar × returns it to its area — it does not close the panel or end its connection), or with Panel: Dock Tab.
  • Close a panel's tab with its own × (a Terminal ends its shell; an FTP / SFTP / SSH tab disconnects).

Drag the divider between the editor and a dock area to resize it, and View → Toggle Panel Auto-Hide collapses the panels until one is shown or focused again.

docs.title: Markdown & HTML preview
docs.text: Open a Markdown or HTML file and turn on View → Toggle Markdown / HTML Preview to see a live preview beside the editor. The preview updates as you type.

docs.title: Git
docs.text:
A built-in Git client, opened as its own tab (Git → Open Git Tab).

  • Local Changes - stage / unstage files (with multi-select), see per-file diffs, and commit (subject + description, amend). Resolve conflicts inline.
  • Commit graph - a lane graph of all branches, with per-commit file lists and diffs; filter or search commits.
  • Branches / tags / stashes / remotes in a navigator, with checkout, create, rename, delete, merge, rebase and more from context menus.
  • Fetch / Pull / Push / Clone, worktrees and LFS - these run your own git.
  • The file panel follows the repository while the Git tab is active.

Info

Local operations use libgit2; network and merge/rebase operations run the git already installed on your system.

docs.title: Hex / Binary Editor
docs.text:
Switch any tab to a hex view with Ctrl+Shift+H (or the command palette).

  • Offset / hex / ASCII columns, with the caret highlighted in both the hex and ASCII columns.
  • Select bytes (Shift+movement or drag), copy them as hex or raw, and find / replace byte sequences (type 48 65 or 4865, or plain text).
  • Insert / overwrite bytes; edits share one undo history with the text view.
  • Optional EBCDIC column, and a configurable bytes-per-row (8 / 16 / 32).
  • Works on large files, and you can compare two files byte-by-byte.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Zume Editor runs on Windows 10/11, macOS and Linux.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
• Microsoft Store (recommended) - search for Zume Editor and install. Updates are delivered automatically.
  • Standalone - a portable ZIP and an installer are also available from the website.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text: • Download the .dmg from the website, open it and drag Zume Editor to Applications. The app is signed and notarized.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
• AppImage - download, chmod +x and run; no installation needed.
  • DEB / RPM - install with your package manager (apt, dnf/rpm).

docs.title: System requirements
docs.text:
• Windows 10 version 1809 or later / Windows 11.
  • macOS (a recent version).
  • A 64-bit Linux desktop with GTK 4.

docs.title: First launch
docs.text: On first launch you get a 30-day free trial - no account needed. When you are ready, buy a subscription on the website and activate in the app. See Activation & Licensing.

docs.title: MAP (Geo Data Conversion)
docs.text: Convert and measure geospatial data without leaving the editor (Tools → Geo).

docs.title: Format conversion
docs.text: Convert between GeoJSON, WKT, KML, GPX and CSV (point data). A neutral model is used internally, so any format converts to any other.

docs.title: Coordinates & transforms
docs.text:
• DMS ↔ decimal degrees, and geohash encode / decode.
  • Slippy-map tiles (z/x/y, Bing quadkey, bounding box).
  • Japan Plane Rectangular CS (平面直角座標系, JGD2011, zones 1-19) ↔ lat/lon.

docs.title: Measurement
docs.text:
• Geodesic length and area of GeoJSON / WKT geometry.

All of this is also available from the command line - see CLI → geo.

docs.title: MCP (AI Integration)
docs.text:
Zume Editor ships a separate program, zume-mcp, that acts as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server. A compatible AI client (such as Claude Desktop or Claude Code) launches it and can then read, create and edit files, query the databases you have configured in the app, and reach external services over HTTPS using API keys you keep inside the app - all through the editor's own, tested engines.

zume-mcp speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio (standard input / output) - it has no window and opens no network port of its own. It is installed alongside the app (next to the executable on Windows, in bin/ on Linux, inside the app folder on macOS).

docs.title: Setting it up
docs.text:
An MCP client launches the server as a command. Point it at zume-mcp:

Windows — portable ZIPWindows — Microsoft Store / MSIXmacOS / Linux

Extract the ZIP to a folder you keep, and use the full path to zume-mcp.exe as the command:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "zume": { "command": "C:\\Tools\\Zume\\zume-mcp.exe", "args": [] }
  }
}

The Store (MSIX) package registers an app execution alias, so after installing you can use the bare name zume-mcp — no path needed:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "zume": { "command": "zume-mcp", "args": [] }
  }
}

(The alias lives on your PATH under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsApps, so it keeps working across updates. zume-cli is aliased the same way.)

Use the full path to zume-mcp inside the app folder (macOS) or the installed bin/zume-mcp (Linux):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "zume": { "command": "/Applications/Zume Editor.app/Contents/MacOS/zume-mcp", "args": [] }
  }
}

Add an env block to the server entry to scope what it can touch — see Restrict what the AI can touch below.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Files, text, hex, search, diff (local disk):

Tool What it does read_file_range Read a bounded byte range of a file (works on very large files) file_info Whether a file exists, and its size in bytes write_file Create a new file, or overwrite / append an existing one (text or hex) search_in_file Literal or regex search; returns matches with offsets / lines extract_strings Printable-ASCII runs with their byte offsets hex_dump A hex + ASCII dump of a byte range find_bytes Every offset of a hex byte pattern (first 64 MiB) patch_bytes Overwrite bytes at an offset in an existing file replace_in_file Replace all literal / regex matches in an existing file and save detect_encoding A file's text encoding and line ending diff_files A line diff of two files (added / removed lines per hunk) search_in_files Literal or regex search across every text file under a directory replace_in_files Replace across a directory; previews by default, applies in one transaction search_large_file Streamed search over a file of any size (byte offsets + preview) compare_folders Compare two directory trees (same / different / left-only / right-only) list_symbols The definitions (functions, types, …) of a source file, with line numbers markdown_to_html Render Markdown (GFM tables, inline formatting) to an HTML document

Map data, conversion, archives, patches, scripting:

Tool What it does geo_convert Convert map data between GeoJSON / WKT / KML / GPX / CSV geo_measure Geodesic length (m) / area (m²) of a GeoJSON or WKT document geo_point geohash, map tile + quadkey + bbox, Japan Plane Rectangular CS, DMS ⇄ decimal geo_reproject Reproject GeoJSON between EPSG CRSs (PROJ) convert_list / convert_run List / run the file-conversion toolbox (base64, JSON ⇄ CSV, timestamps, …) archive_list / archive_extract / archive_create List, extract or create zip / tar / 7z archives patch_bin Apply or create a binary patch (IPS / BPS / UPS / bsdiff / VCDIFF) run_script Run a sandboxed Lua script against a file (preview, or save to write it back)

Security analysis (binary triage / transform / signatures):

Tool What it does entropy Shannon entropy (overall + a windowed sparkline) and the byte histogram — spot packed / encrypted regions transform A CyberChef-style recipe: XOR / ROT / RC4 / base58·85 / hex + the convert toolbox, composed in one pipeline (returns warnings for an ambiguous bare xor:/rc4: key; strict: true refuses one) yara_scan Scan a file, a directory or inline bytes with a practical YARA-rule subset pe_info The structure of a Windows EXE / DLL (PE32 / PE32+): machine, subsystem, timestamp, linker, ASLR / DEP / CFG flags, .NET and Authenticode presence, sections with entropy, imports (incl. delay-load) and exports (incl. forwarders), the resource tree with the version strings, string tables, dialog captions + controls, menu items and the manifest, the PDB path, and any overlay. Structure only — no disassembly elf_info The structure of an ELF executable / shared object (ELF32 / ELF64, either byte order): type, machine, entry, interpreter, segments and sections with entropy, the dynamic section (needed libraries, soname, rpath / runpath), imported / exported symbols with versions, the GNU build id and hardening (PIE, NX stack, RELRO, stack canary, FORTIFY) macho_info The structure of a Mach-O image or fat / universal binary (every slice listed, slice picks one): CPU, file type, header flags, every load command, segments / sections with entropy, dylibs with versions, rpaths, UUID, platform / minimum OS / SDK, the entry, imported / exported symbols, code-signature and encryption presence decompile Decompile a function (or the whole file, capped) of a PE / ELF / Mach-O to C using a local Ghidra, via its headless runner. Off unless ZUME_GHIDRA_HOME points at a Ghidra install (Ghidra is not bundled and needs a JDK). Returns each function's name, address, signature and C; address / symbol picks one (pass an offset from functions / xrefs). Results are cached. Ghidra statically analyses the target; the C is derivative, so reuse only what the licence permits. A managed (.NET) target is routed to il_decompile il_types The type inventory of a .NET / managed assembly (namespace, type name, kind) via a local ILSpy (ilspycmd) — the managed counterpart of functions. Off unless ZUME_ILSPY is set (the path of ilspycmd, or 1 to find it on PATH). Static only; the decompiled IL is close to the source, so reuse only what the licence permits il_decompile Decompile one .NET type to C# (or IL with il), or expand the whole assembly as a .csproj project with out_dir, via ILSpy. Off unless ZUME_ILSPY is set. Pass type (from il_types) or out_dir; a long result spills to a file. Results are cached (ZUME_ILSPY_CACHE) java_types The class inventory of a Java .class / .jar, via the JDK's jar / javap — the Java counterpart of functions. Needs a JDK (JAVA_HOME / PATH). Reads the class files only java_decompile Decompile one Java class to source via a user-provided CFR (set ZUME_CFR to a cfr.jar), or to JVM bytecode via javap (bytecode: true, no CFR needed), or expand a whole jar to a source tree with out_dir. Pass class (from java_types) for a .jar. decompile points a Java target here. Results are cached (ZUME_CFR_CACHE) functions Function boundaries and the call graph of a PE / ELF / Mach-O: each function's address / file offset / size and how it was found, the imports / symbols / functions it calls (with counts), the strings it loads, the data references and the functions that call it; narrowed by target (a name, sub_<hex>, entry or an address). Static and heuristic xrefs Static cross-references of a PE / ELF / Mach-O: every executable section is decoded and each address an instruction uses is classified as an import (PE IAT slot, dll!function), an exported / named symbol, a PLT / stub, a string (with its text), another code address or data; a summary per target plus the referencing instructions, narrowed by target (a name, a string fragment or an address). Static only disassemble A Capstone listing (x86 16/32/64, ARM, Thumb, AArch64) of a byte range of a file or of inline hex bytes. Over a PE / ELF / Mach-O the architecture, the start (the entry point, or the export named by symbol) and the virtual addresses come from the headers, so the offsets pe_info / elf_info / macho_info report can be passed straight in; raw bytes need arch. A decoder only: nothing is loaded, executed or decompiled

Databases (the connections configured in the app, or a SQLite file):

Tool What it does db_list_connections List the saved SQL connections (names only; no passwords) db_schema List a connection's tables / views and their columns db_query Run SQL on a connection and return the result rows nosql_list_connections List the saved Redis / MongoDB connections (by name) nosql_command Run a Redis / MongoDB command and return the result as JSON

Git (a local repository, read-only):

Tool What it does git_status The current branch and the staged / unstaged changes git_log The commit history (id, summary, author, time), newest first git_branches The local branches, with the current one and ahead / behind git_diff The diff of one file (staged or unstaged half)

Remote files (FTP / FTPS / SFTP) (the connections configured in the app):

Tool What it does remote_list_connections List the saved FTP / FTPS / SFTP connections (by name) remote_ls List a remote directory remote_get Download a remote file (to a local file, or return its content) remote_put Upload a local file or inline text to a remote path remote_delete Delete a remote file or empty directory remote_rename Rename / move a remote file remote_mkdir Create a remote directory

Cloud storage (the account you signed in to in the app, or with zume-cli):

Tool What it does cloud_ls List a folder on Dropbox / Google Drive / OneDrive / Box cloud_get Download a file from a connected cloud account cloud_put Upload a local file or inline text to a cloud account

Gen-AI hub:

Tool What it does list_credentials List the names of API keys stored locally http_request Make an HTTPS request to any API, optionally authenticated with a stored key

docs.title: Restrict what the AI can touch (sandbox)
docs.text:
Two environment variables, set on the zume-mcp process, scope what the file tools may do. Both are optional — if you set neither, the tools have full access (the default). Set them in your MCP client's server configuration (an env block) to confine an agent.

Variable Effect ZUME_MCP_ROOTS A list of allowed directories (separated by ; on Windows, : elsewhere). A tool is refused unless its path is inside one of these folders. Symbolic links and .. are resolved first, so a path cannot escape. ZUME_MCP_READONLY 1 / true / yes / on makes the server read-only: every tool that would change a file (write, patch, replace, extract, create, upload, and run_script with save) is refused. Reads still work. 
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "zume": {
      "command": "C:\\Tools\\Zume\\zume-mcp.exe",
      "env": { "ZUME_MCP_ROOTS": "C:\\work\\project", "ZUME_MCP_READONLY": "1" }
    }
  }
}

A refused request comes back as a normal tool error, not a crash. The sandbox covers the local-file tools; the database, remote-file, cloud and http_request tools have their own rules (saved connections, read-only DB profiles, HTTPS only).

docs.title: What the AI can and cannot do
docs.text:
The AI acts only through the tools above.

It can:

  • Read and inspect any file your account can read - text, logs, binaries.
  • Create, overwrite, append and byte-patch files (write_file, replace_in_file, patch_bytes). These are real writes.
  • Query your databases. It can list the SQL connections you configured in the app (db_list_connections), inspect a schema (db_schema) and run SQL (db_query) - against a saved connection by name, or a SQLite file by path. Passwords come from the OS credential store and are never shown to the AI.
  • Operate on remote files over FTP / FTPS / SFTP using the connections you configured in the app (remote_ls / remote_get / remote_put / remote_delete / remote_rename / remote_mkdir). Passwords come from the OS credential store. For SFTP, the server's host key must already be trusted (connect once in the editor); an unknown or changed key is refused, since there is no way to confirm a fingerprint headlessly.
  • Send data out and pull data in over HTTPS (http_request, GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE/HEAD), authenticated with an API key you store locally, referenced by name (the secret is injected by zume-mcp and never returned to the AI).

It cannot (by design):

  • Open a direct database connection the app has not been configured with - db_query only uses your saved connections or a SQLite path you give it.
  • Reach a database over a non-SQL path - http_request is for HTTPS APIs; the DB tools use the editor's SQL engines (SQLite, MySQL / MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQL Server).
  • Use a dedicated cloud-drive tool - cloud upload / download is done with the zume-cli cloud command or the editor's CloudDrive browser, or by calling the provider's HTTPS API through http_request.
  • Reach http://, loopback or local-network URLs - only https:// is allowed.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Point your MCP client at the zume-mcp command. For a client that uses a JSON config (such as Claude Desktop):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "zume-editor": {
      "command": "zume-mcp"
    }
  }
}

On Windows, if zume-mcp is not on your PATH, use the full path, e.g. "command": "C:\\Program Files\\Zume Editor\\zume-mcp.exe".

Microsoft Store (MSIX) build

The Microsoft Store build cannot be used as an MCP server. Its zume-mcp is installed under the protected C:\Program Files\WindowsApps\… folder — a version-specific path that changes with every update and is not on your PATH — so an MCP client cannot launch it. To run the MCP server (or the CLI) on Windows, install the portable ZIP (or the installer build), extract it to a stable folder, and point your client at that zume-mcp.exe, for example:

{ "mcpServers": { "zume": { "command": "C:\\Tools\\Zume\\zume-mcp.exe" } } }

With the Claude Code CLI:

claude mcp add zume -s user -- "C:\Tools\Zume\zume-mcp.exe"

The database tools read the connections you set up in the app's Database workspace. Store API keys for http_request with zume-cli aikey set <name> (see CLI); the AI lists them with list_credentials.

docs.title: Business workflow examples
docs.text:
Each example is one request you make to the AI; it chains the tools itself.

1. Find-and-fix across a code base

"Find every file under src that still calls legacy_init( and change it to init(."

Uses search_in_file + replace_in_file.

2. Export a database table to CSV

"Connect to the reporting database and export this month's orders to orders.csv."

The AI calls db_query on your saved reporting connection (password from the credential store), then write_file to create orders.csv with the rows. A connection you marked read-only in the app will refuse anything but a read query.

3. Enrich a file from a web API

"For each row in orders.csv, look up the status from our REST API and write the result to orders_enriched.csv."

The AI reads the file, calls your API with http_request (authenticated with a stored key), and writes a new file with write_file.

4. Upload a file to a cloud drive

"Upload report.pdf to my Dropbox /reports folder."

The AI reads the file and http_requests the Dropbox content API with a stored token. (For interactive browsing, use zume-cli cloud or the editor's CloudDrive.)

5. Call an external LLM / API with a managed key

"Summarise notes.md with OpenAI and save the summary as summary.md."

Store the key once (zume-cli aikey set openai); the AI calls the LLM with http_request and writes the result with write_file. The key value stays in your local credential store and is never shown to the AI.

6. Work with files on a server

"Download /var/log/app.log from the staging SFTP connection, find the errors, and upload a cleaned copy back as /var/log/app.clean.log."

The AI uses remote_get to download (over your saved staging connection), processes the text, and remote_put to upload the result. The staging host must already be trusted in the editor (SFTP).

docs.title: Let the AI write a Lua script (customise the editor)
docs.text:
A powerful pattern: have the AI write a Zume Lua script for a repetitive edit, then run it in the editor.

"Write a Zume Lua script that aligns the = signs in the selected lines, and save it as align_equals.lua."

The AI drafts the script with the zume API and creates align_equals.lua with write_file. You then run it with Script → Run Lua File, and iterate with the AI until it does exactly what you want.

Note

zume-mcp does not execute Lua - the editor does, where every edit is undoable - so you review and run the script yourself. This keeps you in control while still letting the AI extend the editor for you.

docs.title: Reverse-engineering for app development
docs.text:
The static-analysis tools (pe_info / elf_info / macho_info, extract_strings, functions, xrefs, disassemble, and the optional decompile / il_types / il_decompile) let an AI agent study an existing program and help you build your own application with similar behaviour - the same inventory → locate → read → specify → reimplement workflow a human reverse engineer uses.

Use only on software you are entitled to analyse — and you own what you make

Run these tools only on executables whose licence / EULA permits reverse engineering and that you have the right to analyse — your own builds, open-source binaries, or software whose terms explicitly allow it. Many commercial EULAs prohibit reverse engineering; analysing such software may breach that contract or applicable law. Confirming you have that right is your responsibility.

Decompiled and disassembled output is derivative of the original. Build your application clean-room: work from a written behavioural specification you produce, not by copying the emitted C / C# / IL / assembly into your code.

No liability. Anything you create with this feature is entirely your own responsibility. To the fullest extent permitted by law, the authors and distributors of Zume accept no liability whatsoever for how this feature is used or for anything produced with it.

docs.title: How the pieces fit together
docs.text: Zume, Ghidra and ilspycmd only read the target statically — it is never executed or loaded. Ghidra and ilspycmd are not bundled; they run only when you install them and set ZUME_GHIDRA_HOME / ZUME_ILSPY.

docs.title: Example prompt for Claude Code
docs.text:
Paste this into a Claude Code session that has the zume MCP server connected, replacing the target path and the feature you want:

You have the zume MCP server connected (static binary-analysis tools). 
Target: C:\path\to\target.exe — I confirm I have the right to analyse this
binary (my own build / OSS / a licence that permits reverse engineering).
Work clean-room: produce a behavioural specification and reimplement from it;
do NOT copy decompiled C/C#/IL or disassembly into the new code.

Do this step by step, reporting findings at each stage:
1. Inventory: run pe_info (or elf_info / macho_info) and extract_strings.
   Summarise the feature set, the OS/library APIs it uses, the file formats,
   URLs and error messages, and the UI (dialogs / menus). If pe_info reports
   managed: true, it is a .NET assembly — use il_types instead of functions.
2. Locate: I want to reimplement this feature: <describe the feature>. Use
   extract_strings / search_in_file to find related strings, then functions
   and xrefs (or il_types) to find the functions/types that use them.
3. Read: for the key functions, use disassemble at the offsets functions /
   xrefs reported; optionally decompile (native) or il_decompile (.NET) a
   specific function/type. Explain inputs, outputs, side effects and errors.
4. Specify: write a precise behavioural specification (inputs, outputs,
   formats, edge cases, error conditions) — observed behaviour only.
5. Reimplement: from that specification alone, implement the feature as new
   code in <your language/project>, clean-room. Note anything you could not
   determine statically (it may need runtime observation, which these tools
   do not do).

Keep everything static — never run or load the target. Flag any licensing
concern if the binary embeds third-party libraries whose reimplementation
their licence restricts.

The agent reports at each step; you keep the behavioural specification and the new code, and discard the raw decompiler / disassembler output.

docs.title: Usage notes & cautions
docs.text:
Some tools change files on disk

write_file, patch_bytes and replace_in_file create, overwrite or modify files, and these writes are not undoable from the MCP side (unlike edits made in the editor window). Only let the AI work in folders you trust, and keep backups or use version control.

Database, remote and network access act on your behalf

db_query can read and (unless the connection is read-only) write to your configured databases; the remote_* tools can read, upload, delete and rename files on your configured FTP / SFTP servers; http_request can send data to and fetch data from any HTTPS endpoint using your stored keys. Passwords and key values never reach the AI, but the actions run with your credentials. Configure only the connections and keys you want reachable, connect MCP only to clients you trust, and review what the AI does.

  • It runs with your permissions. zume-mcp can read and write any file your user account can, and reach any database you configured.
  • HTTPS only, body capped. http_request rejects non-https:// URLs, and a response body is truncated at 1 MiB (reported via body_truncated).

docs.title: Privacy & Security
docs.text:
• No telemetry by default. Zume Editor does not send your files or usage data anywhere unless you explicitly opt in.
  • Your data stays local. Files, settings, recent lists and sessions are stored on your own machine.
  • Credentials are protected. SSH, SFTP/FTP, database and cloud passwords are kept in your operating system's secure credential store (Windows Credential Manager, macOS Keychain, Linux Secret Service) - never in plain settings files.
  • License checks contact only our activation server, and only to validate your license. See Activation & Licensing.

For the legal documents, see the website:

  • Terms of Service
  • Privacy Policy
  • Refund Policy

docs.title: 0.30.0 — First public beta
docs.text:
The first public beta of Zume Editor for Windows, macOS and Linux.

Highlights

  • Very large files — open, search, edit and save 10 GB+ files with a near-instant first view, without loading them into RAM.
  • Hex editor — offset / ASCII / EBCDIC columns, byte find & replace, templates, patches (IPS / BPS / UPS / bsdiff / VCDIFF).
  • Git client — stage / commit, branches, a log graph, diffs, conflict resolution, fetch / pull / push, worktrees and LFS.
  • Terminal & SSH shells in a dockable panel, and remote editing over SFTP / FTP / FTPS.
  • Database tools, a two-pane diff & merge, and CSV grid editing.
  • Markdown / HTML live preview, format & encoding conversion, a CLI (zume-cli) and an MCP server for AI agents.
  • Geo data conversion (MAP): DMS, geohash, map tiles, GeoJSON / WKT / KML / GPX, and Japan Plane Rectangular CS.
  • Everyday editing: syntax highlighting, code folding, outline, multi-caret, column (block) mode, search & replace, split view, macros, Lua scripts and session restore.

One license (for the upcoming stable release) covers all three platforms.

docs.title: Beta updates — October 2026
docs.text:
• MCP for AI agents, greatly expanded — the zume-mcp server now exposes most of the editor's engines as tools: cross-file search & replace, map-data conversion (geo), the conversion toolbox, zip/tar archives, binary patches, Markdown→HTML, an outline/symbol list, folder compare, streamed large-file search, Redis/MongoDB, read-only Git, cloud storage, sandboxed Lua scripting, and security analysis (entropy, CyberChef-style transform recipes, a YARA-rule subset scanner). A new sandbox (ZUME_MCP_ROOTS / ZUME_MCP_READONLY) confines what an agent can read or change. See MCP.
  • Markdown preview tables — GFM pipe tables now render as a bordered grid, with bold / italic / code / links inside cells and per-column alignment. HTML tables render in the preview on all platforms.
  • Processing cursor — a busy cursor is shown while a very large file is opening and while an in-file search or replace runs.
  • Dialog polish — long dialog titles no longer wrap or overlap the close button, the Theme dialog's X button and header hover were fixed, and the Settings dialog scrollbar shows a grab cursor.
  • Stability — fixed a crash that could occur after using the Terminal / SSH panel.
  • Various smaller fixes across all platforms.

docs.title: Remote Files (SFTP / FTP / FTPS)
docs.text:
Edit files directly on a remote server.

  1. Remote → Connect - choose the scheme (SFTP, FTP or FTPS) and enter host, port, user and password (or an SSH key for SFTP).
  2. The sidebar becomes a remote browser - click folders to navigate, click a file to open it in a tab.

  3. Save (Ctrl+S) uploads the file back to the server.

  4. Host-key trust - SFTP uses trust-on-first-use; you confirm an unknown key's fingerprint once. FTPS certificate problems ask before continuing.

  5. Saved connections - store connection profiles (never the password unless you choose to save it, and then only in your OS secure store).
  6. Several connections can be open at once, each as its own tab.

See also Terminal & SSH for an SSH shell, and CloudDrive for cloud storage.

docs.title: Security analysis
docs.text: Zume Editor has tools for binary triage, data transforms and signature scanning — useful for reverse engineering, CTFs and authorized security work. Each is also available headlessly to AI agents through the MCP server (the entropy, transform, yara_scan, pe_info, elf_info and macho_info tools).

docs.title: Executable Info (PE / ELF / Mach-O)
docs.text:
Code → Executable Info… reads an executable structurally and lists the result in the results panel. The format is detected from the file's magic:

  • PE (Windows EXE / DLL): the headers and security flags (ASLR / DEP / CFG), every section with its entropy, the imported DLLs and functions, the exports, and the resources a feature inventory needs — the version strings, the string tables, each dialog's caption and controls, the menu items and the manifest — plus the PDB path and any data appended past the last section.
  • ELF (Linux executables and shared objects): type, machine, entry, the interpreter, segments and sections with entropy, the dynamic section (needed libraries, soname, rpath / runpath), imported and exported symbols with their versions, the local symbols when not stripped, the GNU build id, and the hardening the binary carries (PIE, NX stack, RELRO, stack canary, FORTIFY).
  • Mach-O (macOS / iOS images, including fat / universal binaries, whose slices are listed and the first one read): CPU, file type, header flags, every load command, segments and sections with entropy, linked dylibs with versions, rpaths, UUID, platform / minimum OS / SDK, the entry point, imported and exported symbols, and whether the image is code-signed or encrypted.

When the active tab is itself such a file (a binary opened in the hex view), that file is read; otherwise a file picker asks for one. The file is read on a worker, so a large binary does not block the editor (the first 256 MiB are read; a larger file says so in a warning row). Click a row (or press F4) to copy that line to the clipboard; Esc closes the panel.

Rows that name code jump to the disassembly instead: the entry-point line, an exported function, and an executable section or segment. Clicking one opens the file in the hex view at that file offset and runs Hex → Disassemble there with the architecture the file declares (x64, x86, ARM64, ARM / Thumb), so the disassembly panel takes the report's place from that offset; the hex view stays open for browsing.

docs.title: Disassemble Executable
docs.text: Code → Disassemble Executable… goes straight to the listing. It takes the active tab's file when it is a PE / ELF / Mach-O (otherwise a file picker asks), reads the headers, and opens a small dialog asking where to start, prefilled with the entry point's file offset. Type a file offset (0x2D5F0 or decimal) or the name of an exported function (GetProcAddress; a Mach-O name works with or without its leading _) and press Enter: the file opens in the hex view at that offset and the disassembly panel lists the instructions from there, decoded as the architecture the file declares. A name that is not an export, or an offset past the file, is refused with a message. The same decoder is the MCP tool disassemble. Click into the results panel and the keyboard walks it: ↑ / ↓, PageUp / PageDown, Home / End move the highlighted row, Enter activates it (the hex caret moves to that instruction), Esc closes the panel.

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text:
Code → Cross-References… answers "which code uses this": it takes the active tab's executable (or asks for one), opens a small dialog for the target - an import or symbol name (CreateFileW, KERNEL32.dll!CreateFileW), a fragment of a string, a 0x address, or nothing for every reference - and scans every executable section. The results panel lists the targets by reference count (import / symbol / PLT or stub / string / code / data) and then every referencing instruction with its address; clicking a reference row (or pressing F4) opens the file in the hex view at that instruction and disassembles from there. The same scan is the MCP tool xrefs.

The same readers are the MCP tools pe_info, elf_info and macho_info (see MCP). They never load or run the file; disassemble decodes bytes and nothing more. Analyze only binaries whose licence permits it.

docs.title: Decompiler tools — installation
docs.text:
Decompilation is optional and uses tools you install yourself. Zume bundles none of them, downloads nothing, and launches a tool only when you point it at it. Install just the ones you need:

Tool Decompiles Install Enable JDK (Temurin / OpenJDK) prerequisite for Java and Ghidra adoptium.net — Java 17+ set JAVA_HOME, or put java / javap on PATH Ghidra native PE / ELF / Mach-O → C ghidra-sre.org — unzip anywhere (needs a JDK) editor: Tools → Settings → Decompiler (Ghidra); MCP: ZUME_GHIDRA_HOME = the install dir ilspycmd (ILSpy) .NET assembly → C# / IL dotnet tool install -g ilspycmd (needs the .NET runtime) editor: Tools → Settings → Decompiler (.NET / ILSpy); MCP: ZUME_ILSPY = the ilspycmd path, or 1 to find it on PATH CFR Java .class / .jar → Java source download https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/benf/cfr/0.152/cfr-0.152.jar from Maven Central (a single jar; needs a JDK) MCP: ZUME_CFR = the jar path

Notes:

  • javap (JVM bytecode) and jar (class listing) ship with the JDK, so Java class listing and bytecode work with the JDK alone — CFR adds Java source.
  • The ZUME_* variables are read from the MCP server's environment. For the Claude Code CLI that is the env block of the zume entry in ~/.claude.json; restart the client after editing it. Optional result caches: ZUME_GHIDRA_CACHE, ZUME_ILSPY_CACHE, ZUME_CFR_CACHE.
  • Ghidra and ilspycmd are also configurable from the editor's Settings dialog (they drive the editor's own Code → Decompile… commands); the ZUME_* variables drive the MCP tools used from Claude Code. The two are independent.
  • Every tool reads the target statically — it never runs it. Licences differ: Ghidra is Apache-2.0, ilspycmd and CFR are MIT; none is redistributed by Zume. Decompiler output is derivative — see the per-tool sections below and their licence / clean-room warnings before you reuse anything.

docs.title: Decompile (Ghidra)
docs.text:
Zume does not include a decompiler, but it can drive one you already have: Code → Decompile (Ghidra)… turns a function's machine code back into C-like pseudocode using a local Ghidra install. It is optional and off by default - the menu item is greyed out until you point Zume at Ghidra.

Enabling it. Open Tools → Settings…, find the Decompiler (Ghidra) section, click the Ghidra install: row and choose your Ghidra directory (the folder that contains support/analyzeHeadless). Ghidra needs a Java 17+ runtime; Zume finds one on your PATH or JAVA_HOME, so no extra setup is usually needed. Clearing the path disables the feature again.

Using it. With the active tab an executable (or via the file picker), choose Code → Decompile (Ghidra)…, then enter a function - an address (0x180001020, e.g. one functions or xrefs reported), a name, or nothing for the whole file (capped). Zume runs Ghidra headlessly on a background thread (this can take a few minutes the first time) and opens the decompiled C in a read-only tab. Results are cached by the file's size, modification time and your request, so decompiling the same unchanged function again is instant.

The same decompiler is the MCP tool decompile, which is off unless the ZUME_GHIDRA_HOME environment variable points at a Ghidra install (set ZUME_GHIDRA_CACHE to choose its cache directory).

Licence and clean-room

Ghidra statically analyses the binary - it does not run it - but decompiler output is derivative of the original and can resemble its source. Decompile only binaries whose licence permits it, and if you re-implement a feature, work from a behavioural specification, not from the emitted C.

docs.title: Decompile .NET (ILSpy)
docs.text:
A .NET assembly's real code is CIL in its metadata, so Ghidra cannot usefully decompile it. For managed binaries Zume drives ILSpy's command-line tool ilspycmd instead: Code → Decompile (.NET / ILSpy)… turns a type back into C#. Like the Ghidra integration it is optional and off by default - the menu item is greyed out until you point Zume at ilspycmd.

Installing ilspycmd. It is a .NET global tool (the ILSpy desktop app is not needed):

dotnet tool install -g ilspycmd

This needs the .NET runtime and installs ilspycmd (typically %USERPROFILE%\.dotnet\tools\ilspycmd.exe), also putting it on your PATH.

Enabling it. Open Tools → Settings…, find the Decompiler (.NET / ILSpy) section, click the ilspycmd: row and choose the ilspycmd.exe file. The optional IL cache: row chooses where results are cached (leave it unset to use a default location; the folder is created for you on first use). Clearing the path disables the feature again.

Using it. With the active tab a .NET assembly (or via the file picker), choose Code → Decompile (.NET / ILSpy)… and enter a fully qualified type name (e.g. Acme.Core.Engine); leave it empty to list the assembly's types into a tab first, then re-run with one of them. Zume runs ilspycmd on a background thread and opens the decompiled C# in a read-only tab. Results are cached like the Ghidra ones.

The same decompiler is available to MCP clients as il_types (the type inventory, the managed counterpart of functions) and il_decompile (one type to C#, or the whole assembly as a project), off unless the ZUME_ILSPY environment variable is set - the path of ilspycmd, or 1 to find it on PATH (ZUME_ILSPY_CACHE chooses the cache directory). The decompile tool routes a managed target here automatically.

Licence and clean-room

Decompiled C# is very close to the original source (the IL keeps names and structure), so the licence / clean-room caution matters even more than for native code: decompile only assemblies whose licence permits it, and re-implement from a behavioural specification, not from the emitted C#.

docs.title: Decompile Java (javap + CFR)
docs.text:
Java .class / .jar files are JVM bytecode - neither Ghidra nor ILSpy is the right tool. Zume uses the JDK's javap (bytecode) and a user-provided CFR decompiler (Java source) instead, through the MCP tools java_types (list a jar's classes) and java_decompile (one class to Java source, or javap -c bytecode, or a whole jar to a source tree). It is opt-in:

  • javap / jar come from the JDK, found via JAVA_HOME or PATH - the same JDK the Ghidra integration needs. Bytecode and class listing work with the JDK alone.
  • CFR (Java-source decompilation) is a single jar you provide; set the ZUME_CFR environment variable (on the MCP server) to its path. ZUME_CFR_CACHE chooses the cache directory. CFR is MIT-licensed and, like Ghidra and ilspycmd, is not bundled, fetched or linked - Zume only launches the tool you installed.

Installing CFR. It is a single jar - there is nothing to install, just download it once from Maven Central (or the CFR releases):

https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/benf/cfr/0.152/cfr-0.152.jar

Save it anywhere, e.g. C:\Users\<you>\zume-app\cfr\cfr-0.152.jar. A JDK must also be present for java (to run CFR) and javap (bytecode) - the same JDK the Ghidra integration uses.

Enabling it. Set these on the environment of the MCP server (for the CLI, the env block of the zume entry in ~/.claude.json), then restart the client:

"env": {
  "JAVA_HOME": "C:\\Program Files\\Eclipse Adoptium\\jdk-25...-hotspot",
  "ZUME_CFR": "C:\\Users\\<you>\\zume-app\\cfr\\cfr-0.152.jar",
  "ZUME_CFR_CACHE": "C:\\Users\\<you>\\zume-app\\cfr-cache"
}

JAVA_HOME can be omitted if java / javap are already on PATH; class listing and bytecode (javap) then work with the JDK alone, and ZUME_CFR adds Java-source output (CFR). Non-ASCII string literals come back as \uXXXX escapes, which is CFR's normal, lossless output.

The tools read the class files - they never run them.

Licence and clean-room

Decompiled Java is derivative of the original. Decompile only software whose licence / EULA permits reverse engineering and that you have the right to analyse, and re-implement from a behavioural specification, not by copying the emitted Java. Anything you build this way is your own responsibility.

docs.title: Interface recovery (Objective-C / Swift)
docs.text:
Code → Objective-C / Swift Interface… recovers the class interfaces a macOS / iOS Mach-O carries in its Objective-C and Swift runtime metadata — without a decompiler. It reads the __objc_* and __swift5_* sections and writes a header to <app data>/interfaces/<name>.h, opened read-only, listing:

  • Objective-C classes with their superclass and adopted protocols, every instance and class method (- / + with the selector, and the argument and return types where the metadata carries them), the instance variables, the declared properties with their attributes, and the categories that extend a class.
  • Swift types recovered from __swift5_types / __swift5_protos, and the Swift symbols of the symbol table demangled to readable signatures (Module.Type.method(label:) async throws -> T). The demangler is fail-closed: a symbol is demangled correctly or left in its raw _$s… form — never guessed wrong.

When the active tab is such a file it is read; otherwise a file picker asks. A fat / universal binary resolves to the slice read, and pointing the command at a .app or .framework bundle resolves to the Mach-O inside it. Each method row carries the address of its implementation, so activating it (click, or F4) jumps to that method's body in the disassembly, like the Executable Info code rows. The same engine names call sites in Cross-References and in the MCP functions tool — an objc_msgSend site shows the @selector(...) it sends, and a class reference shows the class.

This reads only the metadata Objective-C and Swift leave in the binary for their own runtimes, not the method bodies; it never runs the target. It is most useful on macOS / iOS binaries, where this metadata is richest.

docs.title: YARA Scan
docs.text:
Code → YARA Scan… scans the active document with a set of YARA rules.

The dialog asks for the path to a YARA rules file (.yar / .yara) — not the rules themselves. You write the rules in a file first, then point the dialog at it.

  1. Create a rules file (see the example below) and save it, e.g. C:\rules\malware.yar or ~/rules/strings.yara.
  2. Open the document you want to scan, then run Code → YARA Scan… (it is also in the command palette).
  3. Enter the full path to the rules file and press Enter.
  4. Matches are listed in the results panel as rule $string line N @ offset. Click a row (or press F4) to jump to that line.

The command works on a normal text / code tab (not on large-file, hex or Git tabs).

docs.title: Example rules file
docs.text:
rule suspicious_strings
{
    strings:
        $a  = "cmd.exe /c" nocase
        $b  = "powershell" nocase wide
        $mz = { 4D 5A ?? 00 }              // PE header (?? is a wildcard byte)
        $url = /https?:\/\/[a-z0-9.\-]+/ nocase
    condition:
        $mz and (2 of ($a, $b, $url))
}

docs.title: What is supported
docs.text:
A practical subset of the YARA language:

  • Strings — text ("..."), hex ({ 4D 5A ?? 00 }, with ?? byte and ? nibble wildcards) and regular expressions (/regex/).
  • String modifiers — nocase, wide, ascii, fullword.
  • Conditions — a string name ($a), all of them / any of them / N of them, N of ($a*), #a <op> N (match count), $a at N (match at an offset), filesize <op> N, and / or / not, parentheses, and // … /* … */ comments.

It is not the full libyara engine: modules (pe, hash, math, …), hex jumps ([4-6]) and alternation (( A | B )) are not supported, and a rule that uses them reports a typed error instead of matching.

Inline rules / batch scanning

To paste rules directly, or to scan a whole file or directory at once, use the yara_scan tool over MCP — it accepts the rules as text and a file, a directory or inline bytes as the target.

docs.title: Transform recipes
docs.text:
Code → Apply Convert Recipe… runs a pipeline of transforms over the selection (or the whole document), left to right. Steps are separated by | (or spaces / commas); a step argument follows a colon. For example:

from_base64 | xor:cafe | gunzip

The dialog that opens takes the recipe in its single text field; the hint below the field lists every step the engine accepts, grouped as in the table below, so you do not have to remember them. Type the steps, then press Enter (or OK) to apply; Esc cancels.

docs.title: Every step
docs.text:
Group Steps With an argument xor:<key> (XOR every byte with the repeating key), rc4:<key> (RC4 encrypt / decrypt), rot:<n> (Caesar shift by n) No argument from_hex, to_hex, rot13, not (invert every bit), reverse (reverse the bytes), base58.encode / base58.decode, base85.encode / base85.decode Short names from_base64 = base64.decode, to_base64 = base64.encode, from_base32 / to_base32, gunzip = gzip.decompress, gzip = gzip.compress, url_decode / url_encode Encode base64.encode, base64url.encode, url.encode, qp.encode, html.encode, unicode.escape, rot13, base32.encode Decode base64.decode, base64url.decode, url.decode, qp.decode, html.decode, unicode.unescape, jwt.decode, base32.decode Data timestamp.unixToIso, timestamp.unixMsToIso, timestamp.filetimeToIso, timestamp.isoToUnix, csv.toJson, json.toCsv, csv.toTsv, tsv.toCsv, csv.toMarkdown, csv.toHtml, csv.toSql, json.toYaml, yaml.toJson, json.toToml, toml.toJson, json.toIni, ini.toJson, json.minify, json.pretty, html.toMarkdown Compress gzip.compress, gzip.decompress, zlib.compress, zlib.decompress, bzip2.compress, bzip2.decompress

The Encode / Decode / Data / Compress rows are the converters of File conversion; any converter id works as a step. A key argument (xor: / rc4:) is read as hex bytes when it looks like hex (cafe, deadbeef) and as text otherwise; write hex:cafe or str:cafe to say which explicitly.

A text key that happens to look like hex

Because a bare key is read as hex whenever it is all hex digits, a text password such as cafe, decade or 7a756d65 is taken as bytes, not letters — so rc4:zume uses the text key zume (there are non-hex letters), but rc4:cafe does not use the text cafe. Remove the ambiguity: write rc4:str:<key> for a text/ASCII key (e.g. rc4:str:zume) and rc4:hex:<bytes> — or just the bare hex — for a byte key (e.g. rc4:7a756d65, the hex of zume). The two forms give different keystreams, so matching a key check in a binary (which uses the raw key bytes) means using the hex form of those exact bytes.

Make it an error instead of a guess (strict mode)

To forbid the bare form outright, turn on strict mode in Tools ▸ Settings…, under Transform recipe keys (the strict_transform_keys setting). Every xor:/rc4: key must then carry hex: or str:; a bare key is refused and the recipe is not applied. With strict mode off (the default), a bare key that looks like hex still applies, but the status line warns and names the str:/hex: forms. The transform MCP tool mirrors this: its response always carries a warnings list that flags such a bare key, and a strict: true argument refuses one.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Select the encoded text (or run it on the whole document) and apply:

Recipe What it does from_base64 Decode a Base64 blob from_base64 \| gunzip Decode Base64, then gzip-decompress the result from_hex \| xor:5a Hex-decode, then XOR every byte with 0x5A from_hex \| xor:hex:deadbeef Hex-decode, then XOR with the repeating key DE AD BE EF from_base64 \| rc4:str:s3cret Base64-decode, then RC4-decrypt with the text key s3cret from_hex \| rc4:7a756d65 Hex-decode, then RC4 with the byte key 7A 75 6D 65 (the hex of zume) rot13 ROT13; rot:3 is a Caesar shift of 3 base58.decode Decode a Base58 string (e.g. a wallet address / key) jwt.decode Expand a JWT into its decoded header / payload JSON from_base64 \| xor:cafe \| from_base64 Peel a doubly-encoded, XOR-wrapped payload

The result replaces the selection (or the document) as one undo step, so Ctrl+Z reverts the whole recipe. If a step fails (e.g. input that is not valid Base64), the editor shows which step failed and leaves the text unchanged.

docs.title: Entropy
docs.text: In the Hex / Binary editor, the entropy map and the entropy overview strip show the Shannon entropy of the file per region (0–8 bits/byte), so packed or encrypted areas stand out.
